title: Terraform & Infrastructure as Code: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Why infrastructure is defined as code, declarative versus imperative styles, and the Terraform basics of providers, resources, state, plan/apply, drift and environments, ending with a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Why IaC and Declarative vs Imperative
points: IaC: infrastructure described in version-controlled text files, so environments are reproducible, reviewable in PRs and auditable, instead of built by clicking in a console
Declarative (Terraform, CloudFormation): you state the desired end state and the tool works out the steps; imperative (bash + CLI, SDK scripts): you write the exact ordered steps
Declarative is idempotent: re-running the same config changes nothing if reality already matches; an imperative 'create' script run twice fails or duplicates
Comparison: declarative gives diffs, dependency ordering and destroy for free; imperative gives full control and flexibility but you hand-write ordering, error handling and cleanup
Interview Point: Why is declarative preferred for infrastructure? What does idempotent mean? When is an imperative script still the right tool (one-off tasks, glue steps)?

chapters.title: Providers and Resources
points: Provider: a plugin that translates HCL into API calls for a platform (aws, google, kubernetes); declared in required_providers with a source and version constraint, downloaded by terraform init
Resource block: resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" { bucket = "my-logs" }; type + local name form the address aws_s3_bucket.logs, unique per config
Referencing another resource (aws_s3_bucket.logs.id) creates an implicit dependency graph; depends_on is only for hidden dependencies Terraform cannot see
Data source (data "aws_ami" ...) reads existing infrastructure without managing it; variables take inputs, outputs expose values, both keep config reusable
Interview Point: What does terraform init actually download? Resource vs data source? How does Terraform decide creation order, and when do you need depends_on?

chapters.title: State, Plan and Apply
points: State (terraform.tfstate) maps each config resource address to its real-world ID and attributes; Terraform diffs config vs state vs refreshed reality to decide what to change
terraform plan is a read-only preview showing + create, ~ update in place, -/+ replace (destroy then create), - destroy; terraform apply executes it
terraform plan -out=tfplan then terraform apply tfplan applies exactly the reviewed plan, which is the safe pattern for CI

Remote backend (S3 with native locking via use_lockfile = true, which replaces the now-deprecated DynamoDB lock; or HCP Terraform, formerly Terraform Cloud) shares state across a team and locks it so two applies cannot run at once; state can contain secrets in plaintext, so encrypt it and restrict access
Interview Point: Why must state never be hand-edited or committed to Git? What does state locking prevent? What does -/+ in a plan warn you about?

chapters.title: Everyday Terraform Commands
points: Core loop: terraform init (providers, backend) → fmt → validate (syntax and types, no API calls) → plan → apply
terraform destroy removes everything in state; terraform apply -target=ADDR limits scope but is for emergencies, not routine use
terraform state list and state show ADDR inspect state; state rm stops managing a resource without deleting it; state mv renames an address without recreating it
terraform import ADDR ID (or an import block) brings an existing resource under management, and you must write the matching resource block yourself
Interview Point: Difference between validate and plan? How do you rename a resource without destroying it? How do you adopt a manually created resource?

chapters.title: Drift, Environments and Common Mistakes
points: Drift: real infrastructure changed outside Terraform (console edit); plan refreshes and shows the difference, and apply reverts it to match config, while terraform apply -refresh-only records reality into state without changing resources (terraform plan -refresh-only only previews that update)

Environments: separate state per environment, using a directory per env or a shared module with per-env .tfvars (-var-file=prod.tfvars); workspaces share one backend and config, which suits light separation only
Prefer separate state and backends for prod over workspaces, since a wrong selected workspace is an easy way to apply to prod
Mistakes: committing tfstate or secrets, running apply without reading the plan, unpinned provider versions, one giant state file for everything, editing resources by hand in the console
Interview Point: How do you detect and fix drift? Workspaces vs separate directories for environments? How do you keep a prod apply from hitting the wrong environment?

chapters.title: Terraform and IaC Cheat Sheet
points: Mental model: config = desired state, state = what Terraform believes exists, plan = diff, apply = converge; declarative and idempotent
Workflow: init → fmt → validate → plan -out=tfplan → apply tfplan; destroy to tear down
State tools: state list / show / rm / mv, import ADDR ID, plan -refresh-only for drift; remote backend with locking for teams
Plan symbols: + create, ~ update in place, - destroy, -/+ replace; a replace on a database or disk deserves a pause
Interview Point: Walk through what happens from editing a .tf file to a changed resource, naming config, state, plan, apply and the backend lock.
